name: Tourshi (Armenian Pickled Vegetables)

cookwares.name: 4 wide-mouth 1-quart canning jars with lids and bands

instructions.primary_message: In a small bowl, combine mustard, coriander, peppercorns, allspice, Aleppo pepper, and bay leaves. Stir until evenly combined, then set spice mixture aside.

On a clean work surface, cut vegetables into uniform pieces. For carrots, peel and cut into 1.5-cm sticks about 2 or 8 cm long. For cabbage, cut into quarters, remove core and tender outer leaves, and cut into 2 to 2.5-cm wide wedges lengthwise. For cauliflower, remove stem and cut into large florets. For celery, trim ends and cut into 1.5-cm sticks about 3 or 10 cm long. For green tomatoes, cut into 2.5-cm cubes. For turnips, peel and cut into 1.5-cm sticks about 5 to 8 cm long.

In the bottom of each clean, wide-mouth 1-quart canning jar, place 2 garlic cloves, 2 sprigs parsley, 1 clove, and 2 teaspoons of the spice mixture, then divide the remaining spice mixture evenly among the jars. Add vegetables, sweet peppers, and hot peppers, a few pieces at a time, to the jars, rotating between them, until each jar is filled to within 1.5 cm of rim, packing them as tightly as possible without crushing the contents. (You will have leftover vegetables; save remainder for another use.)

In a nonreactive stainless-steel pot or enameled Dutch oven, combine cider vinegar, water, and salt and bring to boil over high heat. Pour brine into jars until vegetables are covered; discard any remaining brine). Using a spoon, push contents of jars down into brine to ensure everything is submerged, then seal tightly, and invert jars. Let sit at room temperature for 5 days, turning jars over once a day. Refrigerate jars for at least 1 day before serving.
Serve as a snack, as part of a mezze spread, or as a side alongside a main course of your choosing.

schema_metadata.keywords: pickles, pickled vegetables, tourshi, how to pickle vegetables

description: These tangy, lightly-spiced pickled vegetables are an essential part of the Armenian table, and can be made with just about any crisp, edible-when-raw vegetable you can think of.
notes:
Total time, including resting: 6 days 20 min.

Optional or for serving: 4 to 8 fresh hot peppers, such as cayenne, serrano, red jalapeño, or cherry peppers, stemmed and cut into 2.5-cm pieces (optional, to taste; see note)

Optional substitutions: yellow mustard seeds → brown mustard seeds

Notes: Aleppo chile peppers, which have been cultivated in Syria for centuries, are quite mild in terms of heat, with a hint of raisin-y, sun-dried tomato sweetness. Due to the ongoing civil war, true Aleppo pepper from Syria is no longer available for import, but chiles grown in neighboring Turkey are. You can find Aleppo pepper at Middle Eastern markets, or online. Korean gochugaru or 1/4 teaspoon red pepper flakes can be substituted for the Aleppo pepper in this recipe. Take care when adding hot peppers to tourshi, especially if they are on the spicy side; it’s better to err on the side of caution and add more next time around if you want more heat. You can also make this recipe in 2 half-gallon jars, if desired.

Make-ahead and storage: Tourshi can be refrigerated for at least 6 months and up to 1 year, though they will be at their best in the first 6 months: the vegetables will slowly soften over time but will remain edible throughout.
author: Andrew Janjigian
